newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-New Australian airline rumours take flight.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-New Australian airline rumours take flight.

text.p: Australia's aviation market faced more turbulence on Friday as share market rumours grew that Bryan Grey, founder of the failed Compass Airlines, has the backing of an overseas airline to again challenge established locals Ansett and Qantas.

Brokers and aviation analysts said Grey went to investors in Sydney and Melbourne on Wednesday and Thursday this week looking to raise A$100 million to fund the start-up of Aussie Airlines, which hopes to fly nation-wide.
"There is also talk that he has the backing of a couple of Asian airlines," a Melbourne broker said.

"We have heard that he (Grey) is making presentations to institutions and is trying to raise A$100 million -- A$50 million for working capital and A$50 million for security deposit on aircraft," the Melbourne-based broker said.
Australian aviation analysts said Grey did not name the airline that is backing Aussie, but talk centres on Indonesia's Garuda Airlines and Malaysia Air Systems.

However some analysts question the involvement of these two airlines. "Garuda is about to float, so it seems odd that they would want to get involved in a risky venture before they go for an IPO," one Sydney-based analyst said.
Garuda is scheduled to float on the Jakarta stock exchange in 1998, but has made operating losses in the past two years.
"He will need to have someone with deep pockets and a strong commitment to the Australian market," a Melbourne analyst said.
Grey, who was not available for comment, is particularly well known to Australian investors.

Grey's original Compass Airlines took flight in December 1990 after raising A$65 million from investors, 12 months later it was placed in liquidation and left 120,000 Christmas passengers stranded without an airline to fly.
"There is a huge creditability gap with airline start-ups by passengers," another Melbourne-based analyst said.

The Compass banner was resurrected in April 1992 when Southern Cross Holdings issued a prospectus seeking A$50 million, there was a 45 percent shortfall, and in March 1993 Compass II was grounded as Southern Cross was placed in liquidation.
Australia's A$6.0 billion domestic aviation market is dominated by Qantas Airways Ltd and Ansett Airlines Ltd Air New Zealand Ltd.
"Qantas and Ansett will be rigorously defending their market share, both are reducing costs, so the only way Aussie can make it is if it becomes a budget operator," an analyst said.

The talk of a new Australian airline having an overseas airline tie-up was seen as a reason for wiping more than A$210 million off Qantas' market capitalisation. Its share price has fallen seven percent since Tuesday's record high of A$3.21.
On Friday, Qantas shares closed five cents down at A$3.00 on heavy turnover of eight million shares. However, analysts said there may be other reasons for the price fall.

"There are rumours that there is a big sell order on the (Qantas) stock. It has had a good run recently, so it might be people just trying to book some profits," said the Sydney-based aviation analyst.
Qantas shares have risen by 80 percent since hitting their record low in November, making it one of the strongest local stock performers over the past nine months.

Qantas and Aussie have been in talks about sub-leasing facilities from Australia's flag carrier. The government's Federal Airports Corp (FAC) has said it has given both groups an ultimatum to ensure an agreement is reached.

"We have informed the parties in writing that we would want a lease agreement signed by August 31 to allow the beginning of (Aussie) operations in March of next year," FAC spokesman Ted Porter told Reuters.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
